title: Two children, one boy
objectives: See how the way you learn a fact changes the answer.
Condition on the ordered pairs BB, BG, GB and GG, not on counts of boys.
Tell “at least one is a boy” apart from “this child is a boy”.

screens.title: Two children, one boy
screens.prose: A family has two children, and you learn one fact about them. Facts that sound alike can give different answers. What matters is how you came to know the fact.
Each child is a boy or a girl with equal chance, independently. Each cell is one family, elder child first, with chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$. You learn that the elder child is a boy.
screens.question: What is the chance both children are boys?

options.why: That is the chance before the news. Learning about the elder child rules out half the families.
You kept GB, but there the elder child is a girl. Only the top row is left.

hints.text: Which row holds the families with an elder boy?
The top row: BB and BG.
Two families are left, BB and BG, equally likely. One of them has two boys.

feedback.correct: BB is one of the two families left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only the families whose elder child is a boy.

explain.text: Knowing the elder is a boy keeps the top row: BB and BG. They are equally likely, so two boys has chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$. The younger child is still a fair coin.

screens.prose: A different family. This time you only learn that at least one child is a boy. You are not told which.
screens.question: Tap every family that is still possible.

hints.text: Which family has no boy at all?
Only GG has no boy.
Keep BB, BG and GB: each has at least one boy.

feedback.correct: Three families are left: BB, BG and GB.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep every family with a boy in it.

byKey.elder: You kept only the top row, as if the elder were the boy. The boy could be the younger child, as in GB.
byKey.only-bb: You kept only BB. Any family with a boy fits the news, including BG and GB.
byKey.mixed: You left out BB. A family with two boys certainly has at least one.
byKey.r2c2: GG has no boy, so the news rules it out.

explain.text: You kept BB, BG and GB, and crossed out GG. BG and GB are different families: in one the boy is older, in the other younger. Three equally likely families are left.

screens.prose: You kept three families. Each is an **ordered pair**, elder child first, so BG and GB count separately. They stay equally likely after the news.
screens.question: What is $P(\text{two boys} \mid \text{at least one boy})$?

widget.label: Chance of two boys
widget.accept: Any form equal to $\tfrac{1}{3}$, or a decimal that rounds to 0.33.

hints.text: How many families are left, and how many have two boys?
Only BB has two boys.
One of the three equally likely families is BB.

feedback.correct: BB is one of three equally likely families.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count inside the three families that are left.

byKey.half: You split the families into BB and mixed, as if each were half. Mixed comes in two orders, BG and GB.
byKey.prior: That is the chance before the news. GG is now ruled out.

explain.text: One of the three families left is BB, so the chance is $\tfrac{1}{3}$. “The elder is a boy” gave $\tfrac{1}{2}$, because it ruled out GB as well as GG. The two facts sound alike but cut the grid differently.

screens.title: How you learnt it
screens.prose: Another family. You meet one of the two children, chosen at random, and it is a boy. So again at least one is a boy, but you learnt it a different way.
screens.question: What is the chance both children are boys?

hints.text: Which leaves end with you meeting a boy?
Three paths: $\tfrac{1}{4}$ through BB, and $\tfrac{1}{8}$ each through BG and GB.

feedback.correct: Meeting a boy is twice as likely in a BB family.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the paths where you meet a boy, then take the BB share.

byKey.third: You reused the at-least-one count. A BB family shows you a boy every time, a mixed family only half the time.
byKey.prior: That is the chance before you met anyone. GG is ruled out, and BB is favoured.

explain.text: Three paths show you a boy: $\tfrac{1}{4}$ through BB and $\tfrac{1}{8}$ each through BG and GB. So $P(\text{BB} \mid \text{met a boy}) = \dfrac{1/4}{1/2} = \tfrac{1}{2}$. Same fact, different route: the route is part of the evidence.

screens.prose: A friend lists the outcomes as 0, 1 or 2 boys, and gives each chance $\tfrac{1}{3}$. Then “at least one boy” leaves 1 or 2 boys, so two boys gets $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
screens.question: What is the true chance a family has exactly one boy?

hints.text: Which cells have exactly one boy?
BG and GB both have exactly one boy.
Two of the four equally likely cells have exactly one boy.

feedback.correct: One boy happens two ways, BG and GB.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cells with exactly one boy.

byKey.equal: You gave each count of boys equal weight, as your friend did. One boy happens two ways, BG and GB.
byKey.one-cell: You counted one cell. Exactly one boy covers both BG and GB.

explain.text: Exactly one boy covers BG and GB: $\tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{1}{2}$. Zero and two boys have $\tfrac{1}{4}$ each, so the friend's three outcomes are not equally likely. Equal weights belong to the ordered pairs, not to the counts.

screens.prose: A friend says: “At least one is a boy. The other child is a boy or a girl, equally likely. So two boys has chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$.”
screens.question: What goes wrong?

options.text: “The other child” names no definite child: the news does not say which child is the boy

options.why: You accepted “the other child is equally likely a boy or a girl”. That only holds if you know which child is the boy.

options.text: The two children are not independent
options.why: You blamed the children for depending on each other. They are independent; the problem is which child the news is about.
You kept GG. It has no boy, so the news rules it out.

hints.text: In BG, who is “the other child”? In GB?
In BG the other child is the younger; in GB it is the elder.
The news names no child, so “the other child” is not one fixed child. Count the three families instead.

feedback.correct: The news is about the family, not about a particular child.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which child “the other child” refers to in each family.

byKey.fifty: You accepted “the other child is equally likely a boy or a girl”. That holds only once a particular child is known to be a boy, as with the elder.

explain.text: In BG the other child is the younger, in GB the elder: the news names no child. Of the three families left, only BB has two boys, so the chance is $\tfrac{1}{3}$. The friend's $\tfrac{1}{2}$ is right for “the elder is a boy”.

screens.prose: Each family is a string such as `'BG'`, elder first. Filter the families the way each piece of news filters them, then take the share that are `'BB'`.

widget.solution:
import random

def two_boys_at_least_one(families):
    """Keep the families with at least one boy.
    Return the share of those that are 'BB'."""
    kept = [f for f in families if 'B' in f]
    return kept.count('BB') / len(kept)

def two_boys_met_boy(families, met):
    """met[i] is 0 or 1: which child of family i you met.
    Keep the families where that child is a boy.
    Return the share of those that are 'BB'."""
    kept = [f for f, i in zip(families, met) if f[i] == 'B']
    return kept.count('BB') / len(kept)

random.seed(4)
fams = [random.choice('BG') + random.choice('BG')
        for _ in range(20000)]
met = [random.randrange(2) for _ in fams]
print(two_boys_at_least_one(fams))
print(two_boys_met_boy(fams, met))

explain.text: The first filter keeps BB, BG and GB in equal numbers, so the share tends to exactly $\tfrac{1}{3}$; seed 4 prints about 0.330. The second keeps BB every time and a mixed family half the time, so it tends to $\tfrac{1}{2}$; seed 4 prints about 0.492. Same families, different filters.

screens.prose: Write $A$ for “at least one boy”. You found $P(\text{BB} \mid A) = \tfrac{1}{3}$ by counting. Now derive it from the definition.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $= \dfrac{P(\text{BB})}{P(A)}$, since BB has a boy, so $\text{BB} \cap A = \text{BB}$
$= \dfrac{1/4}{1 - P(\text{GG})}$, since $A$ fails only for GG

hints.text: Start from the definition of conditional probability.
Simplify the top first, then the bottom.
Definition, then $\text{BB} \cap A = \text{BB}$, then the complement on the bottom, then the numbers.

feedback.correct: Each line simplifies one part of the fraction.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the definition, then simplify the top, then the bottom.

byKey.comp: The bottom is simplified after the top. Put the line about $\text{BB} \cap A$ first.

explain.text: The top is just $P(\text{BB})$, because two boys already means at least one. The bottom is everything but GG, $\tfrac{3}{4}$. For “the elder is a boy” the bottom would be $\tfrac{1}{2}$, giving $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

screens.prose: A trader makes two trades. Each makes money with chance 0.6, independently. At the end of the day the trader tells you only: “at least one of my trades made money”.
screens.question: Given that report, what is the chance both trades made money?

widget.label: Chance both trades made money
widget.accept: Any form equal to $\tfrac{3}{7}$, or 0.4286 to 3 decimal places.

hints.text: Which cell does the report rule out?
Only loss and loss is ruled out, with chance 0.16.

feedback.correct: Only the loss-loss cell is ruled out.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Remove the outcome the report rules out, then take the share of win-win.

byKey.first: That answers “my first trade made money”. This report could be about either trade.
byKey.prior: That is the chance before the report. Loss-loss is now ruled out.
byKey.half: You treated “the other trade” as a fresh 50:50. The report names no trade, and each wins with chance 0.6.

explain.text: “At least one” rules out only loss-loss, so $P(\text{both} \mid \text{at least one}) = \tfrac{0.36}{0.84} = \tfrac{3}{7} \approx 0.43$. “My first trade made money” keeps the top row and gives 0.6. A trader who chooses which fact to report chooses your filter, and that is where survivorship bias begins.

ideas: The equally likely outcomes are ordered pairs: BB, BG, GB, GG. Counts of boys are not equally likely.
“At least one is a boy” leaves BB, BG and GB, so two boys has chance $\tfrac{1}{3}$. “The elder is a boy” leaves BB and BG: $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
Meeting a boy at random also gives $\tfrac{1}{2}$: how you learnt the fact is part of the evidence.

formula.name: Two boys, given at least one
formula.note: The top is $P(\text{BB})$ because two boys already includes at least one.

summary.trap: “The other child is a boy or a girl, so 1/2” assumes the news named a child. “At least one” names none.

quiz.question: What is the chance all three are boys?

options.why: That is the chance before the news. GGG is ruled out, leaving 7 families.
You fixed one child as the boy and asked about the other two. The news names no child.
You gave 1, 2 and 3 boys equal weight. The ordered families are what is equally likely.

feedback.correct: BBB is one of seven equally likely families left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the 8 ordered families and cross out GGG.

quiz.prose: Two children. You learn that the younger child is a girl.
quiz.question: What is the chance both are girls?

options.why: That answers “at least one is a girl”. Here you know which child is the girl.
That is the chance before the news. Knowing the younger child leaves two families.

feedback.correct: BG and GG are left, equally likely.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the families whose younger child is a girl.

explain.text: Knowing the younger is a girl keeps BG and GG. They are equally likely, so both girls has chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$. The elder child is still a fair coin.

quiz.prose: The trader from the lesson makes two trades, each a win with chance 0.6, independently. Now he picks one of the two at random and tells you: “this one made money”.
quiz.question: What is the chance both made money?

options.why: You treated it as “at least one made money”. He named one trade, so only the other is uncertain.
That is the chance before he spoke. He has told you one trade won.

feedback.correct: He named one trade, so only the other is uncertain.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what is still unknown once he has named a winning trade.

explain.text: He named one trade, so the question is whether the other won: chance 0.6. In Bayes form, $P(\text{report} \mid \text{both}) = 1$ and $P(\text{report} \mid \text{one}) = \tfrac{1}{2}$, giving $\tfrac{0.36}{0.36 + 0.48 \times 0.5} = 0.6$. How he chose what to tell you sets the answer.

quiz.question: Which list gives equally likely outcomes, each one a single result of the two tosses?

options.why: You listed counts of heads. One head happens two ways, HT and TH, so it has chance $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

options.text: Both the same, one of each
options.why: Same and different are equally likely here, but each lumps two results together: HH with TT, HT with TH.

feedback.correct: The ordered pairs are equally likely, each $\tfrac{1}{4}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the list where each entry has chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$.

explain.text: Each ordered pair has chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$. Counts of heads have chances $\tfrac{1}{4}$, $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $\tfrac{1}{4}$. “Same” and “different” happen to be equally likely here, but each lumps two outcomes together.
